causalModel.founding: Villagers hold that a wamasu of Shadowfen lives in the black pond below the bank. The villages leave offerings for the wamasu to keep the seasonal flood back.
causalModel.siteAdvantages: The shrine stands on the bank above the pond where the wamasu is held to live. The bank is at the highest point that the flood reaches.
causalModel.occupantsMotive: Four villages bring the offering in turn each wet season. Each village sets the offering on the stone and leaves quickly.
causalModel.pressures: The offerings have become practical. They now consist of tools and salt. The older villagers find this embarrassing.
causalModel.wouldChangeIf: A flood that came over the bank despite the offerings would end the rotation.

why.what: The district is the strip of bank. It holds the offering shelf and the tally stones.
why.whyHere: The bank stands at the highest point that the flood reaches. It lies above the pond where the wamasu is said to live.
why.whySpot: The bank is firm ground half a metre above black water. A steep rock face rises above it.
why.whyNeighbours: The four villages that bring the offerings lie at a distance from the bank. The bank has no residents.
why.playerPurpose: The district holds the offering shelf, the season's sack and the scorched stone.
why.microGeography: The bank is firm ground half a metre above black water. A steep rock face rises above it.

occupants.cultureRole: The wamasu said to live in the pond below
the headwoman whose village has this year's turn at the shelf

approaches.sequence: The approach runs south-west along the bank. The black pond opens on the right. Then a single dressed stone comes into view on the bank ahead.
approaches.wayfinding: No path reaches the shrine. The carriers follow the bank between the mountain face and the water.

parcels.orientationWhy: The shelf stands broadside to the line of approach along the bank. Carriers can set offerings on it from the bank side.

why.what: The offering shelf is a single old dressed stone. It is loaded with salt, iron and a net.
why.whyHere: The villages leave their offerings here to keep the flood back.
why.whySpot: The shelf stands on the level bank at the water's edge. The flood stops there.
why.whyNeighbours: The tally stones run along the bank to the north-west. The pond lies in front of the shelf.
why.playerPurpose: Villagers leave the offerings on the shelf. Scorch marks show that the creature has answered.
why.microGeography: The ground of the bank is trodden flat beside green-black water. The ground at the water end is burnt.

playerPurpose.note: Practical offerings to a wamasu, left to keep the flood back.
In Offerings Against the Flood the player comes to this bank, where the season's offering sits on the shelf. The flood rose higher this year all the same.

scaleGrounding.loreSource: The catalogue record Shrine of Haynekhtnamet describes an offering shrine. The shrine has no living residents. UESP Lore:Haynekhtnamet is a source for the record. UESP Lore:Wamasu is a second source.
scaleGrounding.why: The shrine has no residents. Carriers from four villages come in turn and leave quickly. The wamasu in the pond is a creature. It is not a resident.

combatSpaces.why: Open bank lies on both sides of the shelf. The pond lies in front of the shelf. A creature that comes out of the water arrives there.

candidates.why: The chosen site is the level bank above the black pond that the record names. It stands at the height that the flood reaches. The bank lies off every registered route. The nearest route is a boat line 613 m away.

candidates.rejectedBecause: The record's own point is on a mountain face that slopes at 42 degrees. All water lies more than 20 m from it.
candidates.why: The record's plotted point lies 115 m north of the pond.

questSockets.why: The socket is the water-side end of the shelf. The offerings there are burnt black.
The socket is the bank in front of the shelf. The carriers of one village set down the season's offering there.

routes.why: The wamasu drags itself out of the east pool here to eat. Its belly has worn a wet mud strip from the water up to the bones and shed scales it leaves.
